theme: Teaching the next generation, remembering God’s works
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 78:1-39. This is a long psalm that retells Israel’s history as a lesson for the next generation. Today’s section covers the exodus and the wilderness. Read it alongside what you have just finished in Numbers.
settingTheScene: Psalm 78 is a psalm of Asaph, and it is the second longest psalm in the Psalter. It is called a “maskil,” a teaching psalm. Its purpose is stated in the first verses: to tell the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, so that they might set their hope in God and not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation. Today’s reading, verses 1 to 39, retells the events of Exodus and Numbers with a focus on Israel’s repeated forgetfulness.
observation: “Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth!” (v. 1).
“We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD” (v. 4).
The purpose: “that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments” (v. 7).
“The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (v. 9).
“They forgot what he had done and the wonders that he had shown them” (v. 11).
“He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap” (v. 13).
“Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert” (v. 17).

“But he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again” (vv. 38-39).
interpretation:
The psalm has a clear structure. It begins with the duty to teach the next generation. Then it gives the story, a long alternating pattern of God’s miracles and Israel’s rebellion. Five times in this section alone, the pattern repeats: God acts, the people forget, and God responds with both discipline and mercy. The psalm reads like a summary of Numbers.

The reason for telling the story is that memory is the cure for unbelief. The people turned back in battle, not because the enemy was strong, but because “they forgot what he had done.” When we forget God’s past faithfulness, we cannot trust his present promises. That is why Moses’ whole book of Deuteronomy is built around the word “remember.”

Look at the pattern in verses 17 to 22. The people ask for food, and they test God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” The question is not wrong in itself. It is that they ask it in unbelief, after seeing him divide the sea and bring water from the rock. They want to see if God can do one more thing. It is a picture of the way we treat God when we hold his past gifts at arm’s length.

The center of the section is verses 38 and 39: “He, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them.” The key word is “atoned.” God’s compassion is not just a feeling. It leads to action. He provides a covering for sin. And his reason is gentle: “He remembered that they were but flesh.” God knows our frailty. He does not forget it.

The psalm ends today’s section with a mixture of warning and comfort. We can be as stubborn as Israel, but God is more patient than we are stubborn. That is the hope we carry as we teach our children the story.
connection: Paul says that the events of the wilderness “took place as examples for us” (1 Corinthians 10:6), and in Romans 15:4 that “whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction.” Jesus quoted this psalm’s words about manna when he said that he is the true bread from heaven (John 6:31). Psalm 103:14 echoes verses 38 and 39: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.” Hebrews 2:17 says that Christ is a merciful high priest who made propitiation for our sins.
application:
Make a list of the works of God that you want to remember, and share one with a child or younger believer this week.

Ask whether there is an area where you are testing God, doubting that he can provide.

Thank God that he remembers you are dust, and that his compassion made atonement.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you tell the next generation of his glorious deeds.
Confess where you forget what he has done.
Thank him for compassion that remembers you are dust.
